extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of humorous/ satirical essays (general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observations relevant to producing short humorous or satirical essays — how to use imagination, tone, and source material, and how to respond to criticism. Draws on examples from dreams, domestic satire, and critics' behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality is impossible / variation not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no originality in them whatever. Human thought is incapable of originality. No man ever yet imagined a new thing--only some variation or extension of an old thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerome argues that writers inevitably alter, vary, or transpose existing material rather than create wholly new ideas (compares thought to a slowly growing tree). Examples: writers who visit the moon or depict future Utopias are essentially reworking familiar elements. Critics' demands for radical originality are therefore unrealistic; authors should expect intertextual echoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for the ordinary reader rather than to impress critics
rubrics_metrics.description: The author contrasts 'ordinary, every-day reader' with the 'high-class critic' who looks for impossible originality and often discards works as unoriginal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerome recounts trying to write a 'classic' piece which he found 'too brilliant' for average readers and which a critic then accused of lacking originality. Practical implication: prioritize clarity, accessibility, and reader engagement over trying to satisfy critics' abstract standards; excessive cleverness may 'wear out' the average reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dreams and dreamlike absurdity as a source of imaginative material
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is only in sleep that true imagination ever stirs within us... In dreams, we fly and wonder not... We go naked, yet are not ashamed... In dreams, there happens that which human language cannot tell."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream-logic permits improbable, surprising, and humorous scenarios (e.g., unscrewing one's legs, a cloak-room demanding legs). For comic writing, invoking dreamlike situations frees the writer from realistic constraints and yields fresh, absurd imagery that can produce humor by contrast with waking expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation — avoid overdoing a conceit or effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "Too much of anything is a mistake... A little enamel paint would have been good... But an entirely and completely enameled home... is, I am convinced, a mistake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through the enamel-paint satire, Jerome shows that exaggeration can be effective in small doses but becomes tiresome or destructive if carried to excess. For humor: cultivate restraint — amplify an idea enough to be comic, but avoid saturating the piece with a single gag or conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and satirize critics and institutions as legitimate comic targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Long dream-episode of a country ruled by critics who condemn all art as unoriginal and reassign artists to 'useful' labor; eventually the public drowns the critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece models satirical treatment of critics themselves: exposing their absurd priorities (obsession with 'wasted time', uniformity of judgment) is both comic material and a defense of artistic activity. Use irony and exaggerated scenarios to critique gatekeepers without losing comic warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextuality and reuse are natural and acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic accuses the author's spring essay of being a collage of classics; the author insists he has not read those writers, implying common cultural inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerome normalizes echoes of earlier writers (Shakespeare, classics). Practical takeaway: borrowing, allusion, and reworking familiar motifs are valid techniques for comic effect; authors need not be paralyzed by fear of plagiarism when creating variations on shared tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a mild, ironic, observational tone for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative voice uses calm cheerfulness, wry observation, and ironic understatement (e.g., family calm at impending hanging; comedic domestic quarrels over enamel paint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay demonstrates that a gently ironic, deadpan delivery — presenting absurdities matter-of-factly — can maximize comic effect. Favor understatement, calm narration of ridiculous events, and wry moral asides rather than shrill or overwrought rhetoric.
